Type.evidence_source: [page/9/Text/4] Our chosen qualitative research design was particularly effective in gaining firsthand knowledge concerning the important processes involved in effective care.

Area.evidence_source: [page/9/Text/6] Participants tended to make negative comparisons between themselves and others based on narrow ideas[page/9/Text/7] of what it was to be a "successful" man. In significant ways, their statements uphold hegemonic masculinity (Connell & Messerschmidt, 2005) in that they reference culturally normative ideals of male behavior such as domination, heterosexuality, drive, autonomy, and self-reliance.[page/9/Text/4] Our findings underscore the need for MHPs to possess and convey therapeutic and supportive (nonjudgmental) attitudes. Crucially, such therapeutic attitudes include those that enable young men to (re)connect with humanity.[page/9/Text/5] Participants recounted their deep sense of connection with, and concomitant therapeutic effectiveness of, specific MHPs. Their accounts focused on perceived human qualities, which they associated with the MHPs' willingness and ability to meaningfully engage with, and thus help, them.[page/9/Text/7] ...any program of care for young suicidal men should include a focus on enabling them to appreciate that there are alternative, equally valid approaches to, and means of, achieving success in life. Accordingly, one effective role of MHPs would be to gently challenge the (self-)limiting constructs and perceptions of young men and replace them with more helpful and realistic views of the wider possibilities open to them. As such, young men could be supported in a process of personal growth and development toward a much more inclusive appreciation of meaningful social participation.[page/9/Text/8] In this context, our findings highlight the need for care to assume an explicitly future-oriented dimension so that young men are supported in the process of identifying (new) meaning in life and obtaining or refining necessary cognitive and other life skills. In the context of developing relevant cognitive resources, our findings highlight the role of behavioral therapies (e.g., CBT and dialectical behavioral therapy).
